questions.question: You are planning a sales dashboard for your manager. What should you decide first?

answerOptions.text: The questions the reader needs answered, then the KPIs that answer them
answerOptions.rationale: Each question becomes one card or table, so the layout follows the questions.

answerOptions.text: Which chart types look the most impressive
answerOptions.rationale: Chart types come after you know the questions they must answer.

answerOptions.text: The colour theme and fonts
answerOptions.rationale: Colour and layout matter, but only once you know what the page must show.

answerOptions.text: How many sheets the workbook should have
answerOptions.rationale: Sheet count does not tell you what a reader needs from the page.

questions.question: The growth card uses the custom format [Color10]▲ 0.0%;[Red]▼ 0.0%;0.0%. What does the second part, [Red]▼ 0.0%, control?

answerOptions.text: How positive numbers are shown
answerOptions.rationale: Positive numbers use the first part, the green ▲.

answerOptions.text: How negative numbers are shown
answerOptions.rationale: A custom format has parts for positive; negative; zero, so the second part is for negatives.

answerOptions.text: How zero is shown
answerOptions.rationale: Zero uses the third part, plain 0.0%.

answerOptions.text: How text in the cell is shown
answerOptions.rationale: This format has no text part; the three parts are positive, negative and zero.

questions.question: On Excel for Mac, which shortcut opens Format Cells so you can type a custom number format?

answerOptions.text: Command + T
answerOptions.rationale: Command T turns a range into a Table.

answerOptions.text: Control + Command + Space
answerOptions.rationale: That opens the Character Viewer, used to find the ▲ and ▼ symbols.

answerOptions.text: Command + 1
answerOptions.rationale: Command 1 opens Format Cells, where you choose Custom.

answerOptions.text: Command + D
answerOptions.rationale: Command D fills a formula down.

questions.question: You have two PivotTables from the same table and one FY slicer. Clicking FY 2025-26 filters only the first PivotTable. How do you fix it?

answerOptions.text: Insert a second FY slicer for the other PivotTable
answerOptions.rationale: Two slicers can disagree, which is the problem you are trying to avoid.

answerOptions.text: Hide the SalesData sheet
answerOptions.rationale: Hiding the data sheet only tidies the dashboard; it does not connect the slicer.

answerOptions.text: Click the Clear Filter button on the slicer
answerOptions.rationale: Clear Filter shows all years again but still controls only one PivotTable.

answerOptions.text: Select the slicer, go to the Slicer tab, click Report Connections and tick the second PivotTable
answerOptions.rationale: Report Connections lets one slicer drive every PivotTable built on the same data.

questions.question: A GROUPBY formula in A5 shows #SPILL! and a dotted border appears below it. What is the usual fix?

answerOptions.text: Clear the cell that is blocking the spill range, such as an old note
answerOptions.rationale: The result needs empty cells to spill into; deleting the blocking cell lets it spill.

answerOptions.text: Wrap the formula in IFERROR
answerOptions.rationale: IFERROR would hide the message without letting the results appear.

answerOptions.text: Convert the data to a PivotTable
answerOptions.rationale: The spill error comes from a blocked range, not from the source data.

answerOptions.text: Update Excel from Help > Check for Updates
answerOptions.rationale: Updating fixes #NAME? on GROUPBY, not a blocked spill range.

questions.question: On your Mac, a GROUPBY formula shows #NAME?. What does the lesson suggest?

answerOptions.text: Delete the cells below the formula
answerOptions.rationale: That fixes #SPILL!, not #NAME?.

answerOptions.text: Turn on AutoSave
answerOptions.rationale: AutoSave affects saving to OneDrive, not which functions Excel knows.

answerOptions.text: Update Excel from Help > Check for Updates, as GROUPBY needs a current Microsoft 365 build
answerOptions.rationale: Older builds do not know GROUPBY, so Excel shows #NAME?.

answerOptions.text: Replace the star (*) in the filter with a plus sign
answerOptions.rationale: The star means AND in the filter and is not the cause of #NAME?.

questions.question: Why does the lesson use Paste > Linked Picture instead of a normal paste to bring the region table onto the dashboard?

answerOptions.text: A linked picture converts the table into fixed values that never change
answerOptions.rationale: It is live; the lesson shows it updating when B4 changes.

answerOptions.text: The picture floats over the cells, ignores column widths and updates when the source data changes
answerOptions.rationale: A linked picture is a live image of the range, so the layout stays intact.

answerOptions.text: A normal paste is not allowed between sheets on a Mac
answerOptions.rationale: Normal paste works; it just breaks the column widths and references.

answerOptions.text: Linked pictures are the only way to add colour to a table
answerOptions.rationale: Colour has nothing to do with it; the reason is layout and live updates.

questions.question: In =SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue],tblSales[FY],"FY 2025-26",tblSales[Region],IF($B$2="All","*",$B$2)), what does the "*" do when B2 is All?

answerOptions.text: It multiplies revenue by the number of regions
answerOptions.rationale: Inside a criteria argument, * is a wildcard, not multiplication.

answerOptions.text: It returns a #CALC! error because no region is called All
answerOptions.rationale: That error happens in GROUPBY with Region=$B$2, not with this SUMIFS.

answerOptions.text: It excludes blank regions only
answerOptions.rationale: The wildcard matches every region name, not just non-blank ones in a special way.

answerOptions.text: It is a wildcard that matches every region, so the card shows the company total
answerOptions.rationale: SUMIFS treats * as "any text", so all regions are included.
